templates.stem: {^who} balances {bar} on a fulcrum. A {w1}-pound weight sits {d1} feet from the fulcrum on one side. On the other side a weight sits {d2} feet from the fulcrum. How heavy is it?

distractors.error: swapped the two distances in the moment equation
assumed equal weights, which only balances at equal distances
gave the moment in foot-pounds instead of a weight
added the quantities instead of using moments

solution_steps: A lever balances when the moments match: weight × distance is equal on both sides.
{w1} × {d1} = {=w1*d1} foot-pounds on the known side.
{=w1*d1} ÷ {d2} = {=w1*d1/d2} pounds on the other side.
templates.recognition_cue: Balance means weight × distance is the same both sides. The weight further from the fulcrum is always the lighter one.

templates.stem: {^who} uses {tool} to lift {loadname}. The effort is applied {earm} feet from the fulcrum, and the load rests {larm} feet from the fulcrum on the other side. If it weighs {load} pounds, what effort force is needed?

distractors.error: put the arms the wrong way round, multiplying the effort instead of reducing it
ignored the lever entirely
added the arms instead of using their ratio
gave a moment in foot-pounds rather than a force

solution_steps: Effort × effort arm = load × load arm.
Load side: {load} × {larm} = {=load*larm} foot-pounds.
{=load*larm} ÷ {earm} = {=load*larm/earm} pounds of effort. The long arm is what makes the job easier.
templates.recognition_cue: A longer effort arm means less effort. If your answer is bigger than the load, you have the arms inverted.

templates.stem: {^who} lifts a {load}-pound load with {rig} that has {strands} supporting strands of rope. Ignoring friction, how much force must be pulled on the free end?

distractors.error: multiplied by the strand count instead of dividing by it
ignored the mechanical advantage of the pulley system
counted one supporting strand too many
assumed every pulley system halves the force

solution_steps: The mechanical advantage of a block and tackle equals the number of strands supporting the load: {strands}.
Effort = load ÷ mechanical advantage.
{load} ÷ {strands} = {=load/strands} pounds.
templates.recognition_cue: Count the rope segments actually holding the load up — that count is the mechanical advantage. The rope you pull only counts if it runs upward.

templates.stem: {^who} uses {rig} with {strands} supporting strands. To raise the load, {rope} feet of rope is pulled through. How high does the load rise?

distractors.error: multiplied instead of dividing by the strand count
assumed the load rises as far as the rope is pulled
assumed every pulley system halves the distance
counted one supporting strand too few

solution_steps: A pulley trades distance for force: the rope moves further than the load, by exactly the mechanical advantage.
With {strands} supporting strands, the load rises {strands} times less than the rope travels.
{rope} ÷ {strands} = {=rope/strands} feet.
templates.recognition_cue: Whatever a machine gains in force it loses in distance. Divide the rope pulled by the strand count to get the lift.

templates.stem: In {machine}, a drive gear with {t1} teeth turns at {rpm1} rpm and meshes with a driven gear of {t2} teeth. How fast does the driven gear turn?

distractors.error: inverted the gear ratio, speeding the big gear up instead of slowing it
assumed meshed gears turn at the same speed
halved the correct speed
gave the gear ratio rather than a speed

solution_steps: Teeth in mesh move at the same rate, so speed × teeth is equal for both gears.
{=rpm1*t1} ÷ {t2} = {=rpm1*t1/t2} rpm. The bigger gear turns slower.
templates.recognition_cue: More teeth means slower. Check the direction of the answer before the arithmetic: driving a larger gear must reduce the speed.

templates.stem: In {machine}, a {small}-tooth gear meshes with a {big}-tooth gear. How many turns does the small gear make while the large gear completes {turnsbig} turns?

distractors.error: inverted the ratio, giving fewer turns for the smaller gear
assumed both gears make the same number of turns
gave the gear ratio rather than a number of turns
added the ratio instead of multiplying by it

solution_steps: The two gears pass the same number of teeth: turns × teeth is equal for both.
Large gear: {turnsbig} × {big} = {=turnsbig*big} teeth passed.
{=turnsbig*big} ÷ {small} = {=turnsbig*big/small} turns of the small gear.
templates.recognition_cue: The smaller gear always turns more times. Set turns × teeth equal on both sides and solve.

templates.stem: {^who} sets up {ramp} {run} feet long that rises {rise} feet. What is its ideal mechanical advantage?

distractors.error: multiplied the dimensions instead of taking their ratio
added the dimensions instead of dividing
arithmetic slip in the division
subtracted the height from the length

solution_steps: For a ramp, mechanical advantage = length along the slope ÷ vertical rise.
{run} ÷ {rise}.
The mechanical advantage is {=run/rise}, so the pushing force is {=run/rise} times smaller than the weight.
templates.recognition_cue: A longer, shallower ramp gives more advantage. Mechanical advantage is always the distance you move divided by the distance the load moves.

templates.stem: {^machine} lifts a {load}-pound load when {effort} pounds of effort is applied. What is its mechanical advantage?

distractors.error: multiplied the forces instead of taking their ratio
subtracted the effort from the load
inverted the ratio, dividing effort by load
arithmetic slip in the division

solution_steps: Mechanical advantage = load ÷ effort.
{load} ÷ {effort}.
The mechanical advantage is {=load/effort}, meaning the machine multiplies your force {=load/effort} times.
templates.recognition_cue: Mechanical advantage is a plain ratio with no units. Load on top, effort underneath — a helpful machine always gives a number above 1.

templates.stem: {^thing} in {place} has a face area of {area} square inches and pushes with a force of {force} pounds. What pressure does it apply?

distractors.error: multiplied force by area instead of dividing
subtracted the area from the force
halved the correct pressure
gave the area rather than the pressure

solution_steps: Pressure = force ÷ area.
{force} pounds ÷ {area} square inches.
{force} ÷ {area} = {=force/area} pounds per square inch.
templates.recognition_cue: Pressure is force spread over an area. Squeeze the same force onto a smaller area and the pressure goes up.

templates.stem: {^thing} weighing {weight} pounds rests on {place} on {feet} feet, each with a contact area of {padarea} square feet. What pressure does each foot put on the floor?

distractors.error: divided by the pad area but forgot the load is shared between {feet} feet
divided the weight between the feet but never divided by the contact area
gave the total weight rather than a pressure
multiplied by the area instead of dividing by it

solution_steps: The weight is shared between {feet} feet: {weight} ÷ {feet} = {=weight/feet} pounds on each.
Each foot spreads that over {padarea} square feet.
{=weight/feet} ÷ {padarea} = {=weight/feet/padarea} pounds per square foot.
templates.recognition_cue: Two divisions, not one: split the load between the supports first, then spread each share over its own contact area.

templates.stem: {^machine} has a small piston of {a1} square inches and a large piston of {a2} square inches. If {f1} pounds is applied to the small piston, what force does the large piston produce?

distractors.error: inverted the area ratio, reducing the force instead of multiplying it
assumed the force passes through unchanged
added the areas instead of using their ratio
multiplied by the large area but never divided by the small one

solution_steps: Pressure is the same throughout the fluid: P = {f1} ÷ {a1} = {=f1/a1} pounds per square inch.
That pressure acts on the whole large piston: F = P × area.
templates.recognition_cue: Same pressure, bigger area, bigger force. Work out the pressure first, then multiply by the other piston's area.

templates.stem: {^machine} has a small piston of {a1} square inches and a large piston of {a2} square inches. The small piston is pushed down {d1} inches. How far does the large piston rise?

distractors.error: inverted the ratio, moving the large piston further than the small one
assumed both pistons move the same distance
multiplied by the small area but never divided by the large one
assumed the distance is always halved

solution_steps: The fluid moved is the same on both sides: area × distance is equal.
Small side: {a1} × {d1} = {=a1*d1} cubic inches of fluid.
{=a1*d1} ÷ {a2} = {=d1*a1/a2} inches of travel on the large piston.
templates.recognition_cue: Hydraulics multiply force and divide distance by the same ratio. The piston that produces the big force always moves the shorter way.

templates.stem: {^thing} on {place} has a spring rate of {k} pounds per inch. How far does it stretch under a {force}-pound load?

distractors.error: multiplied instead of dividing by the spring rate
subtracted the spring rate from the force
halved the correct stretch
gave the spring rate rather than a distance

solution_steps: Hooke's law: force = spring rate × stretch, so stretch = force ÷ rate.
{force} pounds ÷ {k} pounds per inch.
{force} ÷ {k} = {=force/k} inches.
templates.recognition_cue: A spring rate in pounds per inch converts one to the other. Double the load and you double the stretch, as long as the spring is not overloaded.

templates.stem: {^thing} on {place} is supported by {n} identical springs sharing the load equally. If the total load is {load} pounds, how much does each spring carry?

distractors.error: multiplied by the spring count instead of dividing
assumed each spring carries the whole load
counted one spring too many
assumed the load always splits in half

solution_steps: Identical springs sharing a load equally each take the same share.
{load} pounds ÷ {n} springs.
{load} ÷ {n} = {=load/n} pounds per spring.
templates.recognition_cue: Springs side by side share the load and each compresses the same amount. More springs means less on each one.

templates.stem: {^thing} weighing {weight} pounds sits on {surface}. The coefficient of friction between them is {=mu/100|decimal2}. What force is needed to just start it sliding?

distractors.error: used the full weight, as if friction equalled the load
divided by the coefficient instead of multiplying
added the coefficient to the weight
halved the correct friction force

solution_steps: Friction force = coefficient × normal force. On level ground the normal force is the weight.
{=mu/100|decimal2} × {weight} pounds.
That gives {=weight*mu/100} pounds of friction to overcome.
templates.recognition_cue: Friction depends on the coefficient and the weight pressing down, never on how big the contact area is.

templates.stem: It takes {fric} pounds of force to start {thing} weighing {weight} pounds sliding across {surface}. What is the coefficient of friction between them?

distractors.error: divided the wrong way round, weight by force
doubled the correct coefficient
halved the correct coefficient
arithmetic slip in the division

solution_steps: Rearrange friction = coefficient × weight to get coefficient = friction ÷ weight.
{fric} pounds ÷ {weight} pounds. The pounds cancel, so the answer has no units.
{fric} ÷ {weight} = {=fric/weight|decimal2}.
templates.recognition_cue: A coefficient of friction is a bare ratio with no units, and for ordinary surfaces it lands between about 0.1 and 1.0.

templates.stem: {^who} has {bar} {len} feet long with a {w1}-pound weight at one end and a {w2}-pound weight at the other. Treating the bar itself as weightless, how far from the {w1}-pound end is the balance point?

distractors.error: measured from the wrong end
put the balance point at the middle, which only holds for equal weights
divided by one weight instead of the total
arithmetic slip in the division

solution_steps: The balance point sits closer to the heavier end. Total weight is {w1} + {w2} = {=w1+w2} pounds.
Distance from the {w1}-pound end = (other weight × length) ÷ total weight.
templates.recognition_cue: The centre of gravity always sits nearer the heavier weight. Check your answer against that before moving on.

templates.stem: {^who} loads {bar} with three weights measured from the left end: {w1} pounds at 0 feet, {w2} pounds at {d2} feet and {w3} pounds at {d3} feet. Treating the rail as weightless, how far from the left end is the combined centre of gravity?

distractors.error: averaged the positions, ignoring how much each weight matters
left the weight at 0 feet out of the total
put the centre of gravity at the midpoint of the loaded span
arithmetic slip in the division

solution_steps: Multiply each weight by its distance from the left end and add: ({w1} × 0) + ({w2} × {d2}) + ({w3} × {d3}) = {=w2*d2+w3*d3} foot-pounds.
Total weight = {w1} + {w2} + {w3} = {=w1+w2+w3} pounds.
{=w2*d2+w3*d3} ÷ {=w1+w2+w3} = {=(w2*d2+w3*d3)/(w1+w2+w3)} feet from the left end.
templates.recognition_cue: Add up weight × distance for every item, then divide by the total weight. A weight sitting at zero still counts in the denominator.

templates.stem: {who} lifts {thing} weighing {force} pounds straight up through {dist} feet. How much work is done?

distractors.error: added force and distance instead of multiplying them
divided instead of multiplying
halved the work for no reason in the problem
doubled the work

solution_steps: Work = force × distance moved in the direction of the force.
{force} pounds × {dist} feet.
{force} × {dist} = {=force*dist} foot-pounds.
templates.recognition_cue: No movement means no work, however hard you push. Work only counts distance moved along the direction of the force.

templates.stem: {machine} does {work} foot-pounds of work in {secs} seconds. What is its power output?

distractors.error: multiplied by the time instead of dividing by it
gave the work done rather than the rate of doing it
halved the correct power
subtracted the time from the work

solution_steps: Power is the rate of doing work: power = work ÷ time.
{work} foot-pounds ÷ {secs} seconds.
{work} ÷ {secs} = {=work/secs} foot-pounds per second.
templates.recognition_cue: Work is a total; power is work per unit of time. If the question mentions seconds or minutes, it is asking about power.
